newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Outlook for E.Europe turns less rosy - thinktank.
newsitem.headline: Outlook for E.Europe turns less rosy - thinktank.

text.p: The outlook for Central and Eastern European economies, hit by declining cost competitiveness and sluggish demand in the European Union, is not as rosy as estimated earlier this year, a leading research institute said on Friday.

The Vienna Institute for Comparative Economic Studies said it had revised down its forecast for average economic growth in the region in 1997 to two percent, well below the five percent it predicted earlier.
"Once again we see just how fragile the transition process is in Central and Eastern Europe," Peter Havlik, a senior economist at the institute and author of the report said.

The report entitled "Transition Countries' Outlook Falters in 1997" cited internal shocks in Albania, Romania and the Czech Republic as major factors contributing to a slowdown in the region's growth.

The Czech economy -- once the region's model -- slowed down considerably and the crown currency depreciated as financial markets punished it for slow industrial restructuring and soaring trade and fiscal deficits.
"Even seeming success stories like the Czech Republic are not immune, and when the pressures build up to that point, drastic action becomes unavoidable," Havlik said.
The institute revised its growth forecast for the Czech Republic down to 1.5 percent in 1997 from a predicted five percent.
"Growth (in the Czech Republic) in 1998 will hardly be much better as restructuring, corporate governance and competitiveness will not improve overnight," the report said.

Similar imbalances were likely to spark a devaluation in Slovakia and possibly in Poland in 1998, and Russia and Ukraine remained in a precarious state, despite having attained some measure of price stability, it noted.

"These recent repercussions are particularly disturbing because not only are these countries lagging behind the poorer EU countries, but some (of them) have recently even slipped back after initial shocks were apparently overcome," Havlik said.
The outlook for Hungary, Slovenia and to a lesser extent Croatia, was positive thanks to accelerating economic growth.
